cards.title: 1 · Market structures
body: Microeconomics looks at one product, one firm, one household — not the whole nation’s GDP.
**Perfect competition** (the starting model of market structures) needs all of these at once:

cards.title: Many buyers & sellers
body: Nobody is big enough to set the price. Firm is a *price taker*. Its demand curve is a flat line at market P.

cards.title: Homogeneous product
body: Bags of the same grain look alike. No brand loyalty trick.

cards.title: Perfect information
body: Everyone knows the going price. Raise yours and you sell zero.

cards.title: Free entry / exit + mobility
body: Labour and capital can leave a dying use and enter a fat one. No licence wall.

1.1.1 Market Structure
body: Markets are structured or built up of buyers on one side and sellers on the other side.
The behavior of a seller is influenced by the features (structure) of the market in which he/she sells his/her products and the costs of production.
The major organizational features of markets are called the structure of a market or market structure.
Entry can vary from perfectly free or no barrier to totally blocked or no entry.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following are principal assumptions of a perfect competition market structure except:

options.B: Perfect knowledge of prices and quantities

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the characteristics of perfect competition**
Perfect competition is built upon five foundational assumptions: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous (identical) products, perfect information (knowledge of prices/quantities), perfect mobility of resources, and freedom of entry and exit.

**Step 2: Identify the exception**
Heterogeneous (differentiated) products are a central feature of monopolistic competition and oligopoly, not perfect competition.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **Heterogeneous product** is not an assumption of perfect competition.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a perfectly competitive market, each individual seller faces a demand curve that is:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the market power of a single competitor**
In perfect competition, there are many firms selling identical products. No single firm has the power to set the price. They are price takers.

**Step 2: Determine the elasticity**
Since they can sell any amount of output at the prevailing market price, the demand curve they face is perfectly elastic, which is graphically represented as a horizontal line.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The individual demand curve is **Horizontal**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following are characteristics of a monopoly except:

options.A: A product which has no close substitutes

cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the characteristics of a monopoly**
A monopoly is defined by a single seller, a unique product with no close substitutes, and extremely high barriers to entry.

**Step 2: Identify the incorrect characteristic**
Free entry to the market is a characteristic of perfect competition and monopolistic competition. In a monopoly, entry is blocked or highly restricted.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **Free entry to the market** is not a characteristic of a monopoly.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The demand curve facing a monopolist is:

options.C: Downward sloping from left to right
options.D: Upward sloping from left to right

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the relation between monopolist and market**
A monopolist is the sole supplier of the product in the entire market. Therefore, the demand curve facing the monopolist is the market demand curve itself.

**Step 2: Define market demand shape**
Since consumers buy more at lower prices and less at higher prices, the market demand curve slopes downward from left to right.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The monopolist faces a demand curve that is **Downward sloping from left to right**.

cards.title: Demand and supply
body: **Demand:** quantities buyers will take at each price, other things equal. Law: P up → Qd down (usually).
**Supply:** quantities sellers will offer. Law: P up → Qs up.
Move *along* the curve when the good’s own price changes. *Shift* the whole curve when income, tastes, input costs, weather, number of firms, expected future prices change.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Equilibrium Price and Quantity
body: The interaction of demand and supply determines the equilibrium market price and equilibrium quantity of any good or service.
Equilibrium Price: Equilibrium price is the market price where the quantity demanded for a good or service is exactly equal to the quantity of the good or service supplied.
The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity of the good or service that buyers want to buy and the quantity sellers want to sell is the same.
The equilibrium market price is Pe, while the equilibrium quantity is Qe.

options.C: Simultaneous setter of price and quantity
options.D: Firm with no influence on market price

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define market power of a monopolist**
A monopolist has substantial market power due to being the only seller of a product without close substitutes.

**Step 2: Relate to price control**
Because of this control, the monopolist is a price maker/setter. Note that a monopolist cannot set both price and quantity simultaneously; once they set the price, the market demand determines the quantity.

**Step 3: Final Result**
A monopolist is a **Price setter**.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand
body: For some goods and services, a small change in the price affects quantity demanded greatly.
For others, a small change in the price has no appreciable effect on the quantity demanded.
Price elasticity of demand thus measures responsiveness of buyers to the change in the price of the good or service under consideration.
Price elasticity of demand is thus a unitfree measure that is conventionally expressed in terms of positive or absolute value.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Elasticity of Supply
body: Elasticity of supply is the measure of the degree to which quantity supplied responds to changes in one of the variables which affect the quantity supplied.
The interpretation is that an increase in the price of sun eyeglasses by 10 per cent will lead to the increase in the quantity of eyeglasses supplied by 30 per cent.
When price increases from Nakfa 2,000 to Nakfa, 3,000 the percentage change in quantity of maize supplied = (700-400/400) x100 = +75%.
The interpretation is that an increase in the price of maize by10 per cent will increase quantity of maize supplied by 15 per cent.

**Step 1: Define oligopoly**
The prefix 'oligo' means few. An oligopoly is a market structure dominated by a small number of large firms.

**Step 2: Analyze key features**
Because of the small number of sellers, these firms exhibit mutual interdependence, where the actions of one directly affect the others.

**Step 3: Final Result**
An oligopolistic market is characterized by **A few sellers**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the price of milk increases, other things being equal, the law of demand states that:

options.B: The quantity of milk demanded will decrease
options.C: The demand for tea will decrease
options.D: The supply of milk will decrease

cards.why:
**Step 1: State the Law of Demand**
The Law of Demand states that price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship, meaning an increase in price leads to a decrease in the quantity demanded.

**Step 2: Distinguish demand from quantity demanded**
A change in the product's own price causes a change in quantity demanded (a movement along the curve), not a change in demand itself (a shift of the curve).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, **The quantity of milk demanded will decrease**.

cards.title: 1.4 Cost of Production
body: The word ‘Cost’ is commonly used in day to day life and is at the centre of many economic decisions made at the individual, household, firm, national and international level.
Accountants tend to be more concerned with the firm’s finances because they have to keep track of assets and liabilities and evaluate the financial performance.
Economic cost is somewhat different from accounting cost and it is related to the opportunity cost concept.
Although opportunity cost is often hidden, it should be taken into account when making decisions.
Sunk cost is an expenditure that has been made and that cannot be recovered.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the price of commodity 'A' rises and the quantity demanded for commodity 'B' increases, then these commodities must be:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define substitute goods**
Substitutes are goods that can be used in place of one another. When the price of good A increases, consumers switch to the relatively cheaper good B.

**Step 2: Analyze the movement**
An increase in the price of A leads to an increase in the demand (and quantity demanded) of B. This positive cross-price relationship represents substitutes.

**Step 3: Final Result**
These commodities must be **Substitutes**.

**Step 2: Identify the agricultural link**

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: 1.5 Consumer Choice and Demand
body: In general, all individuals face two facts of economic life when they make their choices on consumption of goods and services.
Preferences do not represent actual choices.
In explaining consumer preferences, economists make certain assumptions.

The first assumption is that consumers are able to compare one bundle of goods to other bundle of goods and state either they prefer one to the other or be entirely indifferent between the alternatives.
Other important assumption is that individuals are rational in making decisions and they prefer more than less of the goods and services they consume.

**Step 1: State the definition of Price Elasticity of Demand (Ped)**
Ped measures how responsive consumers are to price changes. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

**Step 2: Interpret the 1 percent concept**
Thus, it yields the percentage change in quantity demanded in response to a 1 percent change in the price of the good itself.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The answer is **The price of a good**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If a 10 percent decrease in the price of a good results in a 30 percent increase in the quantity demanded, the price elasticity of demand is:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the Ped formula**
$$\text{Ped} = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}$$

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
$$\%\Delta Q = 30\%$$
$$\%\Delta P = -10\%$$
$$\text{Ped} = \frac{30\%}{|-10\%|} = 3$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The price elasticity of demand is **3**.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Use the formula for Price Elasticity of Demand (PED): 
$$ PED = rac{\% \Delta Q_d}{\% \Delta P} $$
**Step 2:** Substitute known values:

$$ \% \Delta Q_d = 0.5 \times 10\% = 5\% $$.
Since price decreased, quantity demanded must increase (Law of Demand).

glossary.meaning: Monopoly (one seller), oligopoly (few), monopolistic competition (many but branded).
A market is an institution or a mechanism, through which sellers and buyers interact and engage in the exchange of their goods, services and resources (inputs).
Oligopoly is a market structure where there are a few sellers that produce homogeneous or heterogeneous products.
Compared to a perfect competition, oligopoly is an inefficient market as buyers are charged higher prices.
Each seller has a certain degree of monopoly as it is the only producer of the particular brand or variety of the products.
Monopolistic competition is a market condition in which large numbers of firms (sellers) produce similar but differentiated products.
Oligopoly is a market structure where there are a few sellers that produce homogeneous or heterogeneous products.
Duopoly is a market structure where there are only two sellers of homogenous or differentiated products.
Imperfect competition occurs when there are a number of competing sellers (firms) but the market lacks some or all the features of perfect competition.
Interdependence refers to the degree to which the actions of one firm affect the actions of the others.
Demand is the amount of goods or services consumers are willing and able to purchase at a given price and at a given time.
Perfect market is a theoretical market structure in which there are many buyers and sellers of homogenous products where no single seller or buyer has the power to influence the market price.
Individual demand is the quantity of goods or services demanded by an individual buyer (consumer) at a given price and time.
Market demand is the aggregate or the total amount of quantity demanded by all buyers (consumers).
Demand schedule is a table showing the relationship between the price of a good or service and the quantity of the good or service demanded in a given period of time, other things being equal.
Demand curve is a diagram showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded in a given period of time, other things being equal.
Market price is the main determinant of the quantity demanded for goods and services by consumers.
Supply curve is a curve or a graph that shows the amount of goods or services sold/offered at different prices.

tips.text: In a free market, economic decisions are coordinated by market mechanism.
The operation of the market system allows resources to be allocated, and goods and services to be produced and distributed in accordance with the market forces of demand and supply.
Economic decisions have to be made both by consumers and by producers.
Consumers can choose between a large number of goods and services supplied into the market.
For each good, consumers must decide how much they are willing and able to buy from the market.
Producers must decide how much they are going to produce and supply into the market.
Consumers and producers meet each other in the market.
Coordination between the total quantity demanded by consumers and the total quantity supplied by producers is achieved through the interaction of the market supply and demand.
Economists group different market structures into five categories. These categories are perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and duopoly.
With the exception of perfect competition, all the other market structures are collectively referred to imperfect markets.
Many buyers & sellers: Nobody is big enough to set the price. Firm is a price taker. Its demand curve is a flat line at market P.
Homogeneous product: Bags of the same grain look alike. No brand loyalty trick.
Perfect information: Everyone knows the going price. Raise yours and you sell zero.
Free entry / exit + mobility: Labour and capital can leave a dying use and enter a fat one. No licence wall.

**Step 1: Identify the Formula**

cards.title: 2.1 Merchandising Operations, Control Accounts, and Purchases/Cash Payments Journals (1/3)
body: **Merchandising Business:** A merchandising business is an enterprise whose principal economic activity is purchasing physical goods (merchandise) for resale to customers to generate profit. **Control Account** is a general ledger account that summarizes the overall balance of related detailed accounts in a **Subsidiary Ledger**.

In Grade 10, the study of bookkeeping focused on service-rendering enterprises, such as taxi or cleaning services, where revenue is earned directly from providing intangible services. In contrast, a merchandising business operates in the physical goods sector. These businesses buy finished goods (merchandise) from manufacturers or wholesalers and sell them directly to retailers or final consumers. Consequently, their accounting systems must adapt to track the physical flow of inventory, sales, purchases, freight costs, returns, allowances, and discount periods. This requires more complex bookkeeping structures and ledger operations.

As a business expands and handles hundreds of transactions daily, recording every transaction in a single general journal becomes highly inefficient and prone to errors. To process information systematically, merchandising firms implement **Special Journals**. Special journals are books of original entry designed to record specific types of highly repetitive, identical transactions. These specialized systems save substantial time in journalizing and posting, facilitate the division of labor among multiple accountants, and provide management with organized transactional databases.

For recording credit purchases, businesses employ the **Purchases Journal**. The purchases journal is used exclusively to record the purchase of merchandise on account. If a firm buys supplies, machinery, or any non-merchandise asset on credit, it cannot be recorded in this journal; it must go to the General Journal instead. Similarly, cash purchases of merchandise are excluded here because they involve immediate cash outflow, which belongs in the **Cash Payments Journal** (often called the Cash Disbursements Journal).

cards.title: 2.1 Merchandising Operations, Control Accounts, and Purchases/Cash Payments Journals (2/3)
body: The Cash Payments Journal is designed to record all transactions involving payments or outflows of cash. To streamline the entry process, it features multiple columns for common debits and credits. Typically, there are debit columns for Accounts Payable (to record payments to creditors), Purchases (for cash inventory purchases), and a General (Sundry) column for infrequent debits (e.g., rent expense, drawing, supplies). It also contains credit columns for Cash and Purchase Discounts.

To prevent the general ledger from being overwhelmed with individual accounts for every supplier and customer, firms implement **Subsidiary Ledgers**. A subsidiary ledger contains a detailed group of individual accounts that equal the balance of a single control account in the general ledger. For example, the total of all individual creditor balances in the **Accounts Payable Subsidiary Ledger** must match the single balance of the **Accounts Payable Controlling Account** in the general ledger. This dual system simplifies the general ledger, streamlines the preparation of trial balances, and assists in localizing errors.

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Modern computerized accounting software (ERP) operates on the exact same logic as manual special journals. When a sale is processed, the system automatically writes it to a digital sub-ledger and updates the general ledger control accounts simultaneously.

Unlike other adjustments, the debit (beginning inventory) and credit (ending inventory) extended to the Income Summary are not netted out. Both are extended directly to the Income Statement columns because they represent critical components used in calculating the Cost of Goods Sold.
**Step 3: Final Result**
They are extended to the **Income Statement** column.

cards.title: 2.2 Revenue Generation and Special Journals (Sales and Cash Receipts) (1/3)
body: **Sales Journal:** The sales journal is a specialized book of original entry designed to record only the sale of merchandise on credit (on account). **Cash Receipts Journal:** The cash receipts journal is a specialized book of original entry used to record all transactions that result in the receipt of cash by the business.

Revenue generation is the primary goal of any merchandising business. Sales are conducted either for cash or on credit. Just as credit purchases are segregated into the Purchases Journal, credit sales of merchandise are recorded exclusively in the **Sales Journal**. This journal usually has a single column headed "Accounts Receivable Dr. / Sales Cr." Every single entry in this column increases (debits) Accounts Receivable and increases (credits) Sales. This layout is highly efficient; at the end of the month, the accountant posts only the single column total to both the Accounts Receivable control account (Account 12) and the Sales account (Account 41) in the general ledger, while posting individual customer entries daily to the **Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger**.

Cash sales, on the other hand, represent an immediate cash inflow and are recorded in the **Cash Receipts Journal**. The cash receipts journal must accommodate diverse sources of cash, including collections of accounts receivable, cash sales of merchandise, additional capital investments by the owner, and cash proceeds from bank loans. To record these efficiently, it typically features debit columns for Cash and Sales Discounts, and credit columns for Accounts Receivable, Sales, and a General (Sundry) column for miscellaneous credits.

cards.title: 2.2 Revenue Generation and Special Journals (Sales and Cash Receipts) (2/3)
body: When a merchandising business sells goods on credit, it often offers a **Sales Discount** to encourage customers to pay their outstanding balances quickly. These terms are specified on the invoice, such as $$2/10, n/30$$ (a $$2\%$$ discount is granted if payment is made within 10 days; otherwise, the net balance is due within 30 days). For the seller, a sales discount is a contra-revenue account with a debit normal balance. When a customer takes advantage of this discount, the transaction is recorded in the Cash Receipts Journal by debiting Cash (for the net cash received) and debiting Sales Discounts (for the discount amount), while crediting Accounts Receivable (for the full invoice balance being settled).

To monitor how much money is owed by each individual customer, the business maintains an Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger. Each debtor has an individual account arranged alphabetically. Posting to these individual accounts is performed daily from both the Sales Journal and the Cash Receipts Journal. This ensures that individual customer balances are kept up to date for credit control and billing purposes.

At the end of the fiscal period, the accountant prepares a **Schedule of Accounts Receivable**. This document lists all individual customer balances. Its total sum must equal the balance of the Accounts Receivable control account in the general ledger, verifying the mathematical accuracy of the ledger entries.

cards.title: 2.3 Miscellaneous Entries and the General Journal (1/3)
body: **General Journal:** The general journal is a standard, multi-purpose book of original entry used to record transactions that cannot be entered into any of the specialized journals. **Sales Returns and Allowances:** A contra-revenue account with a debit normal balance used to record the selling price of merchandise returned by customers or price reductions granted to them.

While special journals handle the vast majority of repetitive transactions (credit sales, credit purchases, cash receipts, and cash payments), they do not cover every possible business scenario. A merchandising firm still requires a **General Journal** to act as a clerical safety net for all non-routine transactions. If a transaction does not fit the strict parameters of the four special journals, it must be recorded in the General Journal. Examples of these miscellaneous entries include: adjusting entries, closing entries, reversing entries, purchase of non-merchandise assets (like supplies or equipment) on credit, and purchase/sales returns and allowances when handled on account.

When a customer is dissatisfied with their purchase due to damage, defects, or incorrect specifications, they may return the goods to the seller for a full refund or credit. This transaction is a **Sales Return**. Alternatively, the customer may agree to keep the slightly damaged goods if the seller grants a reduction in the sales price, known as a **Sales Allowance**. To manage these transactions, firms use a single account: **Sales Returns and Allowances**. This is a contra-revenue account with a normal debit balance. It is debited instead of directly debiting Sales to preserve raw historical data for management, allowing them to monitor product quality and customer satisfaction levels.

cards.title: 2.3 Miscellaneous Entries and the General Journal (2/3)
body: Conversely, when the merchandising business itself returns damaged goods to a supplier or receives a price deduction, it is a **Purchase Return and Allowance**. This is a contra-purchase account with a normal credit balance. When these returns and allowances are conducted on credit, they require journalizing in the General Journal because they involve adjusting Accounts Payable and Accounts Receivable balances without any immediate exchange of cash.

To formalize these adjustments, businesses use specific source documents. The buyer requests a reduction in the balance due by issuing a **Debit Memorandum**, which informs the seller that their account payable has been debited (reduced). Upon receiving the request and verifying the claim, the seller issues a **Credit Memorandum**, confirming that they have credited (reduced) the customer's account receivable. These source documents provide the necessary authorization and paper trail for the General Journal entries.

When recording entries in the General Journal that affect control accounts (such as Accounts Payable or Accounts Receivable), the accountant must perform a **dual posting**. The journal entry must identify both the controlling account and the individual subsidiary account. When posted, the amount must be entered in the general ledger control account and also in the individual's subsidiary ledger account. This ensures that both ledgers remain in agreement.

cards.title: 2.4 The Ten-Column Worksheet and Adjustments (1/3)
body: **Worksheet:** A worksheet is a multi-column working paper used by accountants to systematically assemble general ledger balances, plan adjusting entries, compute adjusted balances, and organize data for financial statements. **Prepaid Rent:** An asset representing rent paid in advance, which is gradually consumed and converted into Rent Expense over time.

As the operations of a merchandising business grow more complex, the number of adjusting entries required at the end of a fiscal period increases. To organize these adjustments systematically, accountants expand the standard eight-column worksheet studied in Grade 10 into a **Ten-Column Worksheet**. The ten columns are arranged in five pairs of debit and credit columns: (1) Unadjusted Trial Balance, (2) Adjustments, (3) Adjusted Trial Balance, (4) Income Statement, and (5) Balance Sheet. This structure allows the accountant to prove the mathematical equality of the adjustments before transferring them to the ledger.

The unadjusted trial balance serves as the starting point. However, several accounts do not reflect their true, current values due to unrecorded transactions. Five essential adjustments must be calculated and entered into the Adjustments columns: 1. **Merchandise Inventory:** The general ledger account contains only the opening inventory (the unsold stock from the previous period). The worksheet must eliminate this beginning inventory and record the new ending inventory, determined via a physical count. 2. **Supplies:** The asset account records all supplies purchased. The adjustment transfers the cost of supplies used during the period from the asset account to Supplies Expense. 3.

**Prepaid Insurance:** Over time, the insurance policy expires. The expired portion must be moved from the asset to Insurance Expense. 4. **Prepaid Rent:** The rent paid in advance is consumed. The portion representing the current month's rent is adjusted to Rent Expense. 5. **Depreciation of Equipment:** Fixed assets wear out over time. Depreciation expense is debited, and Accumulated Depreciation (a contra-asset account) is credited.

cards.title: 2.4 The Ten-Column Worksheet and Adjustments (2/3)
body: Adjusting merchandise inventory requires a specific two-step method under the periodic system. First, the beginning inventory is removed from the asset account by debiting **Income Summary** and crediting **Merchandise Inventory** (identified as adjustment `a`). Second, the physical ending inventory is recorded by debiting **Merchandise Inventory** and crediting **Income Summary** (identified as adjustment `b`). These entries are crucial because they place the beginning and ending inventory values directly in the Income Summary account, which is necessary for calculating the Cost of Goods Sold.

Once all adjustments are recorded, the Adjustments columns are totaled to verify that total debits equal total credits. Next, the unadjusted balances are combined with the adjustments to form the **Adjusted Trial Balance**. This combined trial balance is proved again before the individual account balances are extended to either the Income Statement columns (for revenues, costs, and expenses) or the Balance Sheet columns (for assets, liabilities, and capital).

> **💡 Did You Know?**: A physical count of inventory is a legal requirement for most businesses. Even with advanced computer tracking, businesses must physically count their stock at least once a year to account for theft, damage, and waste, a discrepancy known as "inventory shrinkage."

cards.title: 2.5 Adjusting, Closing Entries, and Post-Closing Trial Balance (1/3)
body: **Closing Entries:** Closing entries are journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to transfer the temporary balances of revenue, expense, and drawing accounts to the permanent owner's capital account. **Post-Closing Trial Balance:** A trial balance prepared after all closing entries have been posted, containing only permanent (Balance Sheet) accounts to prove the mathematical equality of ledger debits and credits.

Once the worksheet is completed and the financial statements (Income Statement, Capital Statement, and Balance Sheet) are prepared, the accountant must update the general ledger. This represents the final phase of the accounting cycle. The first step is to record the adjusting entries planned on the worksheet into the General Journal and post them to the ledger. This brings the ledger accounts into agreement with the figures reported on the financial statements.

Next, the accountant must perform the **Closing Process**. General ledger accounts are divided into two main categories: • **Permanent (Real) Accounts:** These accounts carry their ending balances forward to the next fiscal period. They represent assets, liabilities, and the owner's capital account. They are reported on the Balance Sheet. • **Temporary (Nominal) Accounts:** These accounts accumulate financial data for only a single fiscal period. They include revenues, expenses, purchases, sales discounts, and owner drawings. They must be closed (reduced to zero) at the end of the period so they can start the next period with a zero balance.

To close the temporary accounts, the business uses a temporary clearing account called **Income Summary**. The closing process follows four structured steps: 1. **Close Revenue and Contra-Cost Accounts:** Debit all accounts with credit balances (such as Sales, Purchase Returns and Allowances, Purchase Discounts) and credit their total sum to Income Summary. 2. **Close Expense, Cost, and Contra-Revenue Accounts:** Credit all accounts with debit balances (such as Purchases, Freight-In, Salaries Expense, Rent Expense, Sales Returns and Allowances, Sales Discounts) and debit their total sum to Income Summary. 3.

cards.title: 2.5 Adjusting, Closing Entries, and Post-Closing Trial Balance (2/3)
body: **Close Income Summary to Capital:** The balance in the Income Summary account represents the Net Income (if a credit balance) or Net Loss (if a debit balance). Close this account by transferring the balance to the owner's capital account. For Net Income, debit Income Summary and credit Capital. 4. **Close Drawings to Capital:** The owner's drawing account represents a direct reduction in equity, but it is not an expense. Close it by debiting Capital and crediting Drawings.

Once all closing entries are posted, every temporary account in the general ledger will have a zero balance. The only accounts left with active balances are the permanent asset, liability, and capital accounts.

To verify that the ledger remains in balance after this intensive process, the accountant prepares a **Post-Closing Trial Balance**. Since all temporary accounts have been closed, this trial balance will contain only Balance Sheet accounts. Preparing this statement is the final administrative safeguard of the accounting cycle, proving that the general ledger is balanced, accurate, and fully prepared to record the transactions of the next fiscal period.

questions.q: Which of the following accounts **cannot** be reported in the post-closing trial balance?
why: A Post-Closing Trial Balance only contains **permanent (real) accounts**—Assets, Liabilities, and Capital. **Temporary (nominal) accounts**—Revenues, Expenses, and Drawings—are closed at the end of the period and have zero balances.

why:
**Step 1:** Identify the nature of the transaction. A purchase discount is recorded when a company pays its creditors within the discount period.
**Step 2:** Identify the journal for cash outflows. All cash payments are recorded in the **Cash Payment Journal**.

**Conclusion:** Purchase discounts are recorded in the Cash Payment Journal.

questions.q: To close the Income Summary account at the end of a period when a net loss from operations incurred, it is necessary to debit

options.A: Income Summary and credit Capital account.
options.B: Income Summary and credit Expense accounts.
options.C: Revenue accounts and credit Income Summary.
options.D: Capital account and credit Income Summary.
options.E: Drawing account and credit Capital account.

why:
**Step 1:** In a net loss, the Income Summary account has a **Debit balance** (Expenses were higher).
**Step 2:** To 'close' it, we must **Credit** Income Summary for its balance to make it zero.
**Step 3:** The corresponding **Debit** goes to the **Capital account** because a loss reduces the owner's investment.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The purpose of the post- closing trial balance is;

options.D: To test the equality of the debits and credits after the adjusting entries are journalized and posted
options.E: To test the equality of the debits and credits after the temporary accounts are closed

why: A **Post-Closing Trial Balance** is prepared after closing entries are posted. Its purpose is to verify that the ledger is in balance (Debits = Credits) and that only **permanent (Balance Sheet) accounts** remain with balances for the next period.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

options.A: Income Statement Debit; Balance Sheet Credit.
options.B: Income Statement Credit; Balance Sheet Debit.
options.C: Income Statement Credit; Balance Sheet Credit.
options.D: Income Statement Debit; Balance Sheet Debit.

why: In a 10-column worksheet, a **Net Loss** occurs when expenses (Debit) are greater than revenues (Credit). To balance the columns, the loss is added to the Income Statement **Credit** column and the Balance Sheet **Debit** column.

questions.q: One of the following transactions **is not** recorded in the cash payments journal.

options.A: The purchase of a building for cash
options.C: The purchase of supplies for cash
options.D: The purchase of merchandise inventor on account
options.E: The payment of cash for office rent

why: The **Cash Payments Journal** is used to record all transactions involving the outflow of cash. Purchasing merchandise **on account** means buying on credit (no cash is paid immediately), so it is recorded in the **Purchases Journal**, not the cash payments journal.

questions.q: Which of the following transactions for a merchandising business will be recorded in the general journal?

options.A: Purchase of merchandise inventory on account
options.B: Payment of cash for merchandise inventory purchase on account
options.C: Purchase of office equipment on account

why: Special journals handle high-volume transactions: A is recorded in the Purchases Journal, and B is in the Cash Payments Journal. Transactions that don't fit special journals, like **purchasing equipment on account** (C) and **adjusting/closing entries** (D), are recorded in the **General Journal**.

questions.q: Posting from **cash payments journal** is made daily to the:

options.A: appropriate accounts in the accounts payable subsidiary ledger.
options.B: appropriate accounts in the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger.

why: When a business pays its suppliers, it records the transaction in the Cash Payments Journal. To keep individual supplier records up to date, these amounts must be posted **daily** to the specific vendor accounts in the **Accounts Payable Subsidiary Ledger**.
